title: Television Is Terrible at Getting Middle-Aged Women Right
text:
Supported by
Guest Essay
Television Is Terrible at Getting Middle-Aged Women Right
I’ve been watching Sharon Horgan’s HBO series “Youth” with equal parts exasperation and rage.
The show, which finished its eight-episode run early this month, centers on Alex, a 50-something divorced woman re-entering the dating world after she sends her son off to college (though he quickly returns home). At the same time, she’s caring for aging parents and managing a career as a literary agent. She’s squarely in what’s come to be known as the sandwich generation, squeezed between life’s responsibilities.
Rich stuff, particularly from Ms. Horgan, who is the mastermind behind such shows as “Catastrophe,” about a couple trying to make a marriage work after a one-night stand results in pregnancy. And more recently “Bad Sisters,” a delightful dark comedy about a group of sisters plotting to kill their abusive brother-in-law. Again and again, Ms. Horgan has brought complicated, intelligent, fully realized, grown-up women to the screen. A heroic accomplishment, particularly as the number of women making shows in Hollywood continues to decline precipitously. It doesn’t hurt that Ms. Horgan herself — 56, powerful, stylish, divorced, dating a younger man — projects an ideal version of what midlife can look like for women.
But with “Youth” she failed us. Instead of a complex, competent grown-up, Ms. Horgan delivers in Alex an immature, insecure woman, inept at her job, consumed with anxiety about whether men will find her attractive or their friends will think she’s smart. In one episode she drinks too much over lunch, takes a sedative and passes out in the back of a cab for an hour. In another, she drunkenly sleeps with a lecherous former client and does a barefoot walk of shame home. It’s as though someone has stuck Bridget Jones in the body of a 50-year-old and said, here, this is adulthood. Or created a coda to the “Sex and the City” episode in which Carrie shows up for a photo shoot late and hung over and lands on the cover of New York magazine, looking haggard under the headline “Single and Fabulous?” Single and Fabulous question mark? agonizes a horrified Carrie at the magazine stand where she purchases her cigarettes. In this case: Single and Grown-Up question mark?
Messy adult women on our screens are not a new phenomenon. Kerry Washington’s Olivia Pope in “Scandal” tossing back her red wine and sleeping with the president. Sandra Oh’s Eve in “Killing Eve,” engaged in a sexually charged cat-and-mouse game with Jodi Comer’s assassin, Villanelle, while her husband (initially) sits at home oblivious. These characters came after years of women over the age of 40 being relegated to the sitcom roles of the good, exasperated and/or tolerant (but always hot) wife. Centering women as complicated, flawed people, equally averse to commitment as men, felt like a necessary pushback.
And yet even as real-life American women are incredibly high functioning (in 2023, 45 percent of mothers were breadwinners, and 30 percent of women in the United States between the ages of 50 and 64 reported being single), that’s a picture that’s maddeningly rare to get onscreen. Instead, we are offered older actresses (even if they don’t always appear to be so) behaving like 20-somethings. Think Nicole Kidman in “Babygirl,” who timidly slides into a BDSM relationship with her male intern. (It’s the timidity, not the relationship, that I found so frustrating.) The silly “Sex and the City” reboot “And Just Like That.” There is no competence to back up the chaos. No learned wisdom. Instead, it’s just a hot mess.
An accurate, and far more entertaining, version of this middle period of life might have delivered us a woman inundated with male attention, uncertain that the one relationship, should she invest in it, is worth the effort. Perhaps she prefers to spend time with female friends or — gasp! — alone. (When women don’t remarry or marry after 50, it’s not because the option isn’t available — it’s often because staying single is preferable.) How about a story of women being weeded out of the job market by artificial intelligence that filters out résumés with too much experience. Maybe a story line that focuses on the pressure to erase any evidence of age from our bodies. Or how about a series just depicting a woman having fun? I’m happy to report, there is much to be had. Or all of the above at once. This time period in a woman’s life is so fascinating and extreme and full of contradictions. We are at the same time incredibly powerful and diminished. Confident and ignored.
